source.title: Archetypal SAE: Adaptive and Stable Dictionary Learning for Concept Extraction in Large Vision Models
source.authors: Thomas Fel; E. Lubana; Jacob S. Prince; Matthew Kowal; Victor Boutin; Isabel Papadimitriou; Binxu Wang; Martin Wattenberg; Demba E. Ba; Talia Konkle

record.tranche_reason: The study investigates SAE dictionary stability and concept quality in vision models, but does not test whether SAE residuals are linearly predictable, scale across SAE sizes, affect model computation, or arise from training artifacts in the sense of the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports reconstruction metrics and describes the tokenwise reconstruction-error distribution for one Archetypal SAE, but does not compare residual predictability or error contexts across SAE sizes. The reconstruction-error distribution is recorded as a related finding under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study is about dictionary instability across seeds and archetypal (convex-hull) constraints for SAEs on vision models. It never analyses the SAE error vector: no linear prediction of residuals, no per-token error comparison across SAE sizes, no loss-under-splicing versus random-error control, no split into linear and nonlinear error, and no circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term. Reconstruction R2 is reported only as an aggregate fidelity metric across SAE variants. The original dark-matter paper is not cited.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that standard SAEs are unstable across runs, and that archetypal constraints greatly improve stability. The relaxed variant RA-SAE matches standard SAE reconstruction. Both improve plausibility and identifiability benchmarks and dictionary structure in large vision models.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies archetypal and relaxed archetypal SAE dictionaries, not the original dark-matter analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: For one Archetypal SAE on DINOv2, reconstruction error is roughly uniform across tokens, except the CLS token, which has the highest error (Fig. 10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction error in ViTs concentrates on the CLS token rather than on patch tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: On DINOv2 at 90% sparsity with 2000 concepts, R2 is 83.94 (Vanilla), 89.52 (TopK), 89.92 (JumpReLU) and 89.34 (RA-SAE). About 10% of variance stays unexplained across architectures, including the constrained one (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unexplained variance in vision-model SAEs is similar across SAE architectures, including archetypal constraints. This is an aggregate fidelity metric, not a decomposition of dark matter.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The study does not analyze the structure or functional effects of SAE residuals relevant to the claim. The reported tokenwise error description is for one setting and has no stated uncertainty.

untested.parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is linearly predictable from the input activation; not examined.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, same failing contexts, and persistence with scale. Dictionary-size sweeps appear only for the plausibility score (Table 2), not for error.
Downstream loss when reconstructions are spliced in, versus random errors of equal norm; not examined.
Linear versus nonlinear error components and how learnable each is; not examined.
Loss of circuit or steering behaviour without the error term; not examined.
Whether dark matter shrinks with better architectures or objectives. Only aggregate R2 is compared across Vanilla, TopK, JumpReLU and RA-SAE; the error is not decomposed.

record.verdict_notes: There is no closer relation option, so 'discusses' is kept. The paper concerns SAE reconstruction and dictionary quality generally but does not engage the dark-matter claim or cite its original source; 'cites_only' would also be inaccurate. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of the input activation.
Whether per-token error norms are predictable across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
Whether SAE reconstruction errors harm model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether linear and nonlinear error components differ in feature content or dictionary learnability.
Whether omitting SAE error terms from circuits or steering loses model behavior.
Whether dark matter is mainly a training artifact, or whether it shrinks with alternative SAE objectives, architectures, or end-to-end training.

rows.subject: DINOv2
rows.operation_detail: Describes the tokenwise distribution of reconstruction error for an Archetypal SAE.
rows.measure: Distribution of reconstruction error across tokens
rows.value: Uniformly distributed across tokens, except the CLS token, which has the highest reconstruction error
rows.note: The paper does not compare this distribution across SAE sizes or measure predictability from input activations.
rows.check: This is a qualitative reading of Figure 10 for one RA/Archetypal SAE on DINOv2-B with 4 registers. There is no baseline, no comparison across SAE sizes and no predictability analysis, so it cannot show any version's effect. Keep it as a descriptive row linked to no version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
